sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, one word or phrase, match).

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) Religious reforms among Sikhs were started in the twentieth century. (b) The Khalsa College of Amritsar was founded in 1892.
questions.answer: (a) False – they began at the end of the 19th century. (b) True.

questions.q: Answer in one word: (a) In which year was Sati declared illegal? (b) In which year was the Sharda Act passed?
Fill in the blanks: In the ______ century and especially after 1919 the ______ national movement became the main propagator of social reforms.

Fill in the blanks: Numerous individuals, reform societies and religious organisations worked hard to spread ______ among women, to prevent ______ of young children, to bring women out of purdah and to enforce monogamy.

Answer in a phrase: (a) Why did reformers take recourse to propaganda in Indian languages? (b) Why did reformers use novels, dramas, short stories and poetry?
questions.answer: (a) To reach the masses. (b) To spread their ideas widely among common people.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in about 25 words.

questions.q: State any two features of the Muhammadan Literary Society.
questions.answer: It promoted discussion of religious, social and political questions in the light of modern ideas, encouraged upper and middle class Muslims to adopt Western education and played a role in Muslim unity.

or.q: Explain the role of Aligarh Muslim University.
or.answer: It grew out of Sir Syed's Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College as the central educational institution of Indian Muslims to promote modern Western science and culture without weakening ties with Islam.

questions.q: Examine any two specific features of Sir Syed's reform.
questions.answer: He urged Muslims to take modern education and be broad-minded and tolerant, reconciled Islam with science and rationalism, and opposed purdah, polygamy and easy divorce.

questions.q: What were the principles of the Brahmo Samaj?
questions.answer: Belief in one God, opposition to idol worship, sacrifices and offerings, condemnation of sati, human dignity, unity of religions and equality regardless of caste or creed.

questions.q: State the objectives of the Arya Samaj.
questions.answer: To propagate the true knowledge of the Vedas, oppose idolatry, polytheism, ritual and caste practices, promote education (DAV institutions) and women's uplift, and perform suddhi.

questions.q: Why is Swami Vivekananda remembered?
questions.answer: He carried Ramakrishna's message to the West, promoted Vedanta and the oneness of religions, said service to the poor is the highest religion and founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897.

questions.q: Name two laws passed for women in the 19th century.
questions.answer: Sati declared illegal (1829); widow remarriage legalised (1856); marriageable age raised (1860); inter-caste marriage law (1872).

questions.q: Why were only a few laws related to women passed by the British government?
questions.answer: The British wanted to appease the orthodox upper sections of society.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 40–50 words.

questions.q: Explain any three works by which Raja Ram Mohan Roy sought to improve the condition of women.
questions.answer: He campaigned against sati for years, citing scriptures and appealing to compassion, until it was banned in 1829; he demanded education and property inheritance rights and advocated widow remarriage; and he opposed polygamy, child marriage and the notion that women were inferior.

or.q: Explain three social evils which Brahmo Samaj sought to abolish.
or.answer: Sati, idolatry and sacrificial rites, caste rigidity, child marriage and polygamy.

questions.q: Examine the contribution of the Prarthana Samaj.
questions.answer: Founded in Bombay by Dr Atmaram Pandurang, it aimed at rational worship and social reform: inter-caste dining and marriage, widow remarriage and uplift of women and the depressed classes. Ranade and Bhandarkar led it; it believed in the unity of God but did not insist on a break with caste or idols.

questions.q: Describe the contribution of Annie Besant and the Theosophical Society.
questions.answer: The Society promoted study of ancient religions and philosophies and universal brotherhood; under Annie Besant it gave Indians pride in their heritage, fought untouchability, supported women's upliftment, founded the Central Hindu College (later BHU) and started the Home Rule League in 1916.

questions.q: Write a note on the Aligarh Movement.
questions.answer: Started by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan, it promoted modern Western education among Muslims without weakening ties with Islam through the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875), gave Muslims a common language Urdu and a press, and supported women's education and removal of purdah.

questions.q: Describe the reforms among Parsis and Sikhs.
questions.answer: Parsis: the Rehnumai Mazdayasan Sabha (1851) with Naoroji Furdonji and Dadabhai Naoroji and the journal Rast Goftar modernised customs and promoted girls' education. Sikhs: Singh Sabhas (1870) and the Khalsa College at Amritsar (1892) promoted Gurmukhi and Punjabi; the Akali movement won control of gurdwaras in 1925.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 150–200 words.

questions.q: Explain the life and works of Swami Ramakrishna Paramhans.
questions.answer: Gadadhar Chattopadhyaya (1836–86) was a poor Brahmin priest with only elementary education who dedicated himself to God. He believed there are many roads to God and that service of man is service of God, since man is the embodiment of God; sectarianism had no place in his teachings, and he saw divinity in humanity. His pupil Narendranath Datta (Swami Vivekananda) carried his message to America and Europe and founded the Ramakrishna Mission (1897) for social service, stressing oneness of religions and Vedanta.

questions.q: Discuss the role of Raja Ram Mohan Roy and the Brahmo Samaj in the awakening of India.
questions.answer: Roy is called the harbinger of the modern age. He studied several religions, promoted English education, condemned idol worship and priestly practices and founded the Brahmo Sabha (1828), open to all, which opposed idols, sacrifices and sati. He worked against sati until 1829, against caste, polygamy and child marriage, and for women's education and inheritance. Debendranath Tagore and Keshub Sen carried on; the Samaj stood for individual freedom, national unity and democracy and was the first organised vehicle of national awakening, with great impact on Bengal.

questions.q: Describe the contribution of Swami Dayanand and the Arya Samaj to religious and social reform.
questions.answer: Dayanand (Mool Shankar, 1824–83) founded the Arya Samaj in Bombay in 1875, holding that the Vedas contain all knowledge; he opposed idolatry, ritual, priesthood and caste, supported women's education and widow remarriage and wrote Satyarth Prakash in Hindi. DAV schools (Lahore, 1886; Lala Hansraj) and Shraddhananda's Gurukul (1902) spread education; suddhi reconverted Hindus; the Samaj built self-respect and nationalism in northern India.

questions.q: Discuss the efforts of Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan in the reform of the Muslim community.
questions.answer: He realised Muslims must adapt to British rule through modern education. He interpreted the Quran in light of reason and science, urged tolerance and unity of Hindus and Muslims, founded schools, had Western books translated into Urdu and set up the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh (1875), later Aligarh Muslim University. The Aligarh Movement gave Muslims a common language Urdu and a press; he denounced purdah, polygamy and easy divorce and wanted women educated.

questions.q: Write about the impact of the reform movements on Indian society.
questions.answer: Laws were passed against sati (1829), infanticide, for widow remarriage (1856), inter-caste marriage (1872) and the Sharda Act (1929). After 1919 the national movement propagated reform using Indian languages, novels, drama, the press and the cinema; women's education grew and purdah and child marriage declined, women joined the freedom struggle and many superstitions disappeared.
